brief_extract:
National Executive Committee. * * * *
The official launching of the Trust took place at 20, Regent Street, London, S.W.1, on November 28th, 1945, at a large Press gathering including prominent electrical and educational personages. THE RIGHT HON.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding the homemaking reputation of British women.
brief_extract: There should be one voltage throughout the entire country, and women were needed to help in getting these things done. The women of Britain were known all over the world as excellent homemakers. They would be better homemakers when the drudgery represented by the open fire, by the hearth brush and by all those dreary things connected with coal were eliminated.

brief_context: Mentioned as a family that electrical progress will help animate.
brief_extract: More women were needed in public life — on Local Authorities, in Parliament and the many social welfare organisations. When with a good electrical installation the housework of a flat could be done in about an hour the housewife would be able to join these important organisations helping to make this England a real lively, animated family, an achievement wrought in war by much overwork, when women put up with old-fashioned homes and yet did a good job. They should no longer have to cope with dirt, smoke and inconvenience, and these Scholarships and Travelling Exhibitions would teach a more universal use of this gift of Electricity.

brief_extract:
SIR STAFFORD CRIPPS, K.C., M.P.,
President of the Board of Trade, at the Birthday Luncheon. THIS Association was launched 21 years ago by members of the Women's Engineering Society who had a vision of what this comparatively modern development of mobile power and heat called Electricity could do to benefit women in this country. It was to form a two-way channel between the electrical industry and the domestic consumer.

brief_extract: What the E.A.W. considered good, convenient and attractive for the British housewife would appeal to housewives abroad, and thus its work along the line of design would help the country in another direction. In the tremendous programme of house-building is a great opportunity to introduce the electric servant into all of them, and though the E.A.W.

brief_context: Context of improving the lives of women in Britain.
article_title: Response by MISS CAROLINE HASLETT, C.B.E.
brief_extract: Its original conviction of the necessity for relating science to everyday life and giving women a share in that development had been progressively strengthened. To-day the Electrical Industry had in its hand a great gift which would ameliorate the lot of Britain's women by giving them labour-saving homes and surroundings, and would do much to offset the cumulative strain of war. A great age was foreshadowed for women, and therefore for the whole nation, the features of which were happy, healthy families, citizen communities with women freed from household drudgery to take part in Local and National Government.

brief_context: Mentioned in relation to national defence during the war.
article_title: Advertisement: Women's Auxiliary Air Force (W.A.A.F.) - Electrical Skills in the Air Force
brief_extract: We served as electricians, radiographers, telephonists, and teleprinter operators. As skilled Radar operators we played a vital part in the defence of Britain. Such trades were once thought to be outside women's province.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding the mobilization of women workers.
article_title: COULD INDUSTRY HAVE DONE WITHOUT US?
brief_extract: We made it. Higher proportion of women mobilised in Britain than in any other country. 1,851,000 in munitions industries.

brief_context: Defence of these islands using Radar.
brief_extract: That required real intelligence, real "expertise," a real grasp of technical principles on the part of the everyday operator. Sir Robert had had the privilege of suggesting well before the war that the Radar equipment for the defence of these islands could be better operated by women than by the men who would be available. He suggested as a first experimental project the training of three women as the first Radar operators in the world.

brief_context: Air Defences of this country depended on Radar operators.
brief_extract: The experiment was very successful, even more successful than he had hoped, and the decision for such recruitment was taken in the early months of the war. Sufficient emphasis has never been laid on the fact that at the crux of the Radar war the Air Defences of this country depended primarily on a group of Radar operators, some two-thirds of whom were girls. They did the work superlatively well in the two Battles of Britain.

brief_context: Mentioned in the context of the Battles of Britain.
brief_extract: Sufficient emphasis has never been laid on the fact that at the crux of the Radar war the Air Defences of this country depended primarily on a group of Radar operators, some two-thirds of whom were girls. brief_context: Scientific institution where Humphry Davy delivered lectures on science.
brief_extract:
He built the first voltaic pile, or electric battery, as we now call it. In 1810 a young and very popular professor of chemistry, Humphry Davy, lecturing at the Royal Institution, founded in 1799, said that the first plan was that the Royal Institution should be:

"A School for promulgating the Knowledge or Use of important Mechanical Inventions; for connecting the Views of Men of Science and Artisans, and for laying open the general Principles, and teaching the Application of all Improvements in the Sciences, in their connexion with the Arts of Life. The great feature of the establishment was intended to be a Collection of Models, of Mechanical Contrivances, and of all Implements employed in the Common Purposes of Life, in their most perfect state; and it was designed to diffuse the knowledge of these, and point out their applications as connected with the general doctrines of science, by courses of Public Lectures."

The Royal Institution tried to do for General Science what E.D.A.

brief_extract:
The leisure of the higher female classes is so great, and their influence in society so strong, that it is almost a duty, that they should endeavour to awaken and keep alive, a love of improvement and instruction. Humphry Davy was at that time a very popular and handsome bachelor of 31, and two years later he married a wealthy widow of the “ higher classes of society.” Although he may amuse us, he has much to teach us, for he lived at a time when England and France were at war. A question has been raised in the House of Commons which will, it is hoped, find a satisfac- tory solution in the April Budget. It is the proposed removal of the Purchase Tax on electric kettles, irons and washing machines, as their use economises both in fuel and in the housewife’s time, while eliminating much house- hold drudgery and consequent unnecessary fatigue.

brief_context: Where a survey among housewives was conducted.
brief_extract: . A recent survey among repre- sentative cross-sections of house- wives in the Home Counties states that “all 10,000,000 of her deserve a far greater measure of consideration than has been ac- corded in the past,” that she is eager “ to accept what science and technical skill can offer to ease her arduous burden,” and is anxious for more of the cul- tural amenities of life. The aver- age young housewife is willing to allocate as much as £60 on domestic electrical equipment from a £350 a year income, and £25 in lower income groups, and even the older woman, who may be more conservative and already possesses some equipment, is willing to spend £30 and £11 respectively in the same income groups.

brief_context: Mentioned for ceding claim to seats on the Council.
brief_extract: An enormous range of problems political and practical were explored, from the disposal of war criminals to details of emoluments of the permanent staff, even such questions as third party risks in case the staff should run over each other or the citizens of the United States. The work rose in a steep crescendo both in quantity and contentiousness from the amiable opening speeches and the generous gestures of Canada and New Zealand in ceding their claim to seats on the Councils when the votes were tied, to the acrimonious later debates on the admission of the World Federation of Trade Unions in a consultative capacity (the Russians objected, unsuccessfully, to the inclusion of the American Federation of Labour), and on the question whether Refugees should be compelled against their will to return to their country of origin, upon which the Russians insisted, again unsuccessfully. The documents piled up, reaching eventually over four million pages; and there was the social side, banquets and receptions.

APRIL, 1946

JUST IDEAS
FACTS catch up with ideas so quickly nowadays that it is well to be informed of labour-saving devices in their earliest stages. From America comes the suggestion of an electric service trolley with boiling plate and grill for light cooking and hot cupboard underneath. There is also room on top for a carving board and a little extra space ; a rack for towels and napkins ; a place for cutlery ; a moving shelf for a saucepan ; a lower shelf for vegetable or meat storage ; a drawer for vinegar and other condiments.

brief_context: Location of a fully automatic heat pump installation being described.
brief_extract: Moreover, low-grade coal is used at the power station to provide the electrical energy for the heat pump, whereas that for a coal-fired boiler is of high quality. Fully automatic control is being installed at Norwich to dispense with the need for attendance, and the advantages over coal-fired boilers can there- fore be deduced. A comparison between the size of the old boiler house and the present pump house strikingly demonstrates the saving in space.

brief_context: Location where the heat pump was constructed.
brief_extract: The installation of a central heat pump at a riverside with transmission of heated water to other buildings in a circuit is an economical form of district heating, which compares favourably with district heating schemes from a central generating station. The Norwich Heat Pump was constructed from whatever material was readily available at a difficult time, and the pump has therefore been fulfilling a very practical purpose of efficient and economic heating. Its experimental value will be seen in the results to be published from the records kept over a specified period.

brief_context: Origin of hosiery representatives and trade unions visiting the exhibition.
brief_extract: Good lighting is also important in the training section of the exhibition where entrants to the industry are taught their craft under modern conditions by scientific methods of tuition instead of being placed alongside an older worker and just left to "pick up" the process as best they may. During its three weeks' existence the exhibition was visited by Working Parties investigating conditions in other industries, and by representatives of hosiery manufacturers and trades unions from all over England and Scotland. The final impression should be one of the importance of environment in relation to efficiency, not only the cold efficiency of machines but the integration of all the factors that make a good work-place, such as good clear vision resulting in high individual efficiency and increased output; satisfactory work-places in which the natural response of work-people to efforts successfully made on their behalf leads to better relations between workers and managements and hence to better conservation and recruitment of labour.

GOVERNMENT PUBLICATIONS
A Central Institute of Management (H.M.S.O., 3d.), the report of a Committee appointed by the Board of Trade to formulate detailed proposals for setting up a Central Institute for all questions connected with management, recommended the establishment of a professional body whose functions would be "to provide a centre for the study of management, to carry out research and to disseminate information on the subject of management, to encourage and advise on schemes of training in management, to work in close cooperation with those existing management bodies which are effective in their own specialist fields, and, generally, to take all possible steps to assist in raising the standards of management practice in this country." Miss Caroline Haslett was a member of the Committee. Domestic Fuel Policy (H.M.S.O., 1/-), the report by the Fuel & Power Advisory Council appointed to advise on the development and utilisation of the fuel and power resources of the country in the national interest, begins with a quotation from 150 years ago: "I am not without hopes that at some future period houses in England will become as celebrated for warmth and comfort as they are now for neatness," outlines the present unsatisfactory position, and makes recommendations for improving it. The New Towns Bill (H.M.S.O., 9d.) and the Second Interim Report of the New Towns Committee (H.M.S.O., 6d.) give the up-to-date Government provisions for the creation of new towns.

brief_extract: Osborn (Faber & Faber, 12/6) shows how modern urban centres safeguarded by green belts can promote efficient modern industry and a healthy, balanced life. brief_context: Context of a New Britain after the war.
brief_extract:
OCTOBER, 1946

Communities For Work and Living

BACKGROUND TO THE NEW TOWNS ACT

Throughout the war years the houses, towns and cities that were to arise with the coming of peace were the subject of discussion and reports, and the centre of many hopes. To-day "squat-ting" seems to be the most featured of the activities related to housing, and one tends to become bewildered and disil-lusioned that a New Britain has not come into being straight away. It is well, in these circum-stances, to trace the various steps in the Government plans for re-housing, and to consider the many complex factors which hinder or expedite their imple-mentation.

location_standardised: 20 Regent Street, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Former residence of the E.A.W. Headquarters.
brief_extract:
It is in that spirit that we approach our task."

While suggesting a wide range of amenities and stressing the importance of planning ahead, the Final Report of the same Committee gives a wise caution to those who want to go too far and too fast in a limited space of time: —
"What can be provided must de-pend on the material economic situa-tion, the success of the full employ-ment policy, and a rising standard of national income derived from a rising standard of production, to which we think the living and working condi-tions in the new towns will contribute."

NEW E.A.W. HEADQUARTERS

After fourteen years' happy residence at 20, Regent Street, the E.A.W. Headquarters has regretfully had to seek other ac-commodation owing to the dis-posal of the Crown Lease of this property.

brief_extract: Thomas Johnston, at that time Secretary of State for Scotland, now Chairman of the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board, put through a measure known as "The Hydro-Electric Development (Scotland) Act, 1943," which, so far as the Scottish Highlands are concerned, is the greatest contribution to the problem of rehabilitation which has yet been made. The Act provides for, and makes possible, the development of Scotland's abundant water power resources, which are mainly located in the Highland area, in a manner which enables the benefits to accrue more effectively to the Highlands themselves than was formerly possible. The Act, which gives power to the Hydro-Electric Board to develop hydro-electric resources, transmit and distribute electricity, makes it a condition that first priority must be given to all these remote and isolated areas which I have just described to you.

brief_extract:
The New Towns Bill was presented to Parliament in April and incorporated, subject to modification, provisions of the Town and Country Planning Act, 1944, and the New Towns Act was passed by Parliament in August. These are the facts in chronological order, and they provide the general framework for the more human aspects of the matter, such as Stevenage and Crawley—Three Bridges, which are naturally better known to the public. Planned Decentralisation
The terms of Reference of the New Towns Committee were:
“To consider the general questions of the establishment, development, organisation and administration that will arise in the promotion of New Towns in furtherance of a policy of planned decentralisation from congested urban areas; and in accordance therewith to suggest guiding principles in which such Towns should be established and developed as self-contained and balanced communities for work and living.”
Two types of new town were considered—either entirely new, planned and built where previously there was only a scattered and rural population, or major extensions of existing small towns.

article_title: Magnitude of the Problem and Speed of Construction
brief_extract:
This involves expanding the building industry to a personnel of about 1,250,000 by the fourth year, and the civil engineering industry in proportion. Under this programme building is expected to work up to a peak production of between 400,000 and 500,000 houses a year for six to eight years from the middle of 1949, in addition to repairs and other building work in that period."

"The number of people who will ultimately be re-housed in new towns of both classes (including those in the London Region) may be of the order of two and a half to three millions, and possibly more."

The speed in reaching this goal is governed by many limitations, among them the allocation of manpower in relation to other demands, the housing and general maintenance of these building workers over a long period, and the synchronisation of employment facilities with the provision of domestic dwellings for the inhabitants of the new town. "There is also the more elastic factor of the right speed to achieve the healthy integration of a balanced community."

Variety in Employment, Interests and Income Groups

Democratic principles are the basis of all recommendations :

"Variety of employment as between industrial and other occupations is necessary to achieve a social balance; a variety of types of industry is desirable for many reasons, though there will be special cases where a single industry will predominate."

Recommendations are also made for a balance of income groups and of varied interests, and the avoidance of one-class neighbourhoods.

It will be held at the Training College of Domestic Arts for South Wales and Monmouthshire on October 19th when the Principal will welcome the delegates.

brief_extract:
E.A.W. Annual Conference, 1947
The date of the 1947 Annual Conference is May 14th-16th and the place is Southport. The programme will include addresses on subjects of scientific and general interest, a Luncheon and Reception, and visits to places of special electrical interest.

article_title: [Appointment of Miss Haslett to Advisory Committee]
brief_extract: As the magazine goes to press, Miss Haslett has just been appointed by Mr. Lewis Silkin, M.P., Minister of Town and Country Planning, a member of the Advisory Committee in connection with setting up of the new town: Crawley-Three Bridges.
